## Why This Project Matters {background-color="#FFF4E6"}

<br>

- Today's quantum computers only have a **few qubits** to work with
- Every instruction (**gate**) has a chance of introducing an **error**
- Qubits that aren't next to each other need **extra gates** just to talk to each other
- **Shorter programs = more trustworthy results**
- Our project looks for gates that **don't need to be there**

::: notes
This is the "so what" slide - keep it plain and quick, this is meant to hook interest, not explain everything.
Avoid heavy jargon here, save definitions for the next slide.
:::

## What is a Quantum Circuit? {background-color="#F7F9FC"}

A quantum program is usually written as a circuit.

- **Qubits** = wires (like bits, but quantum)
- **Gates** = instructions applied left to right
- A qubit can be **0**, **1**, or **both at once**

## Why This Is Worth Optimizing {background-color="#FFE9E9"}

<br>

- Quantum programs are often made **"controlled"** — only run if an extra qubit is 1
- Naive approach: control **every single gate** in the program (expensive!)
- **Our idea:** if part of a circuit **undoes** an earlier part, we may only need to control the **middle piece**
- This hidden pattern is exactly what we're hunting for

::: notes
Keep this as a teaser, not the full deep-dive comparison - just enough to show there's a real payoff worth chasing.
A fuller version with concrete gate counts is a good topic for a follow-up presentation once we have results.
:::

## Our Project Aim {background-color="#EAF3FF"}

<br>

- Build a tool that **automatically finds** this hidden pattern in a circuit
- Use it to build **cheaper controlled versions** of that circuit
- Start with the **simplest case** first, and build up from there
- Using **existing quantum tools**, not starting from scratch
